title: The King and the Onion
summary: A merchant claims onions are a rare delicacy and sells them to Akbar for gold. Birbal ensures the merchant receives poetic repayment with garlic.
full_text:
A cunning traveler from the western deserts arrived at the court of Emperor Akbar, carrying a basket of ordinary red onions. In those days, onions were rarely grown in the imperial capital. The traveler presented them as a rare, celestial root endowed with magical flavor and medicinal vitality.

Akbar tasted a cooked onion, found its savory sweetness delightful, and rewarded the traveler with one hundred gold mohurs!

Seeing this extraordinary fortune, an envious merchant named Hiralal thought: 'If the Emperor gave one hundred gold coins for ordinary onions, what will he give for garlic, which is twice as pungent and flavorful?'

Hiralal spent his life savings purchasing three cartloads of the finest garlic bulbs and presented them to Emperor Akbar, claiming they were the supreme medicinal roots of the Himalayas.

Akbar tasted the garlic and found it immensely flavorful. Pleased, the Emperor asked Birbal: 'What reward should we bestow upon this merchant who brought such an aromatic wonder?'

Birbal, seeing through Hiralal's greedy scheme, smiled pleasantly: 'Sire, gold and silver are common metals. For a man who brings such a celestial delicacy, we must reward him with the most precious, rare treasure currently residing in the imperial palace!'

Hiralal's heart leaped with joy. He imagined rubies, emeralds, or a palace estate!

'What is this treasure, Birbal?' Akbar asked.

'Sire,' Birbal answered, 'the most precious rarity in our palace is the basket of celestial red onions that we purchased yesterday for a hundred gold coins! Let us bestow the entire basket of onions upon this worthy merchant!'

Akbar agreed with delight. Hiralal was handed the basket of common onions in exchange for his three cartloads of garlic!

The greedy merchant went home with tears in his eyes and onions in his hands, having learned that greed that mimics another's success invariably reaps its own folly.

Believing rumors and flattery without proof
